image-alt.name: Images must have alternate text
image-alt.description: Informative elements are missing an alt attribute, so screen reader users receive no information about the image.
image-alt.whyItMatters: Screen readers announce images through their alt text. Without it, users hear the file name or nothing at all, losing content that sighted users get visually.
commonCauses: CMS image uploads without alt fields filled
Decorative images not marked with empty alt
image-alt.recommendedFix: Add a concise alt attribute describing the image's purpose. Use alt="" only for purely decorative images.
image-alt.developerGuidance: Audit every . If the image conveys information, describe it. If it is decorative, use alt="" so assistive technology skips it.

color-contrast.name: Elements must meet minimum color contrast
color-contrast.description: Text does not have sufficient contrast against its background, making it hard or impossible to read for low-vision users.
color-contrast.whyItMatters: Roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color vision deficiency, and low contrast affects everyone in bright sunlight or on low-quality displays.
commonCauses: Light gray text on white backgrounds
Brand colors used without contrast checking
color-contrast.recommendedFix: Ensure a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold).
color-contrast.developerGuidance: Add contrast checks to your design tokens. Tools like the WebAIM contrast checker or browser devtools can verify each pair.

link-name.name: Links must have discernible text
link-name.description: Links have no accessible name, so screen reader users cannot tell where the link leads.
link-name.whyItMatters: Screen reader users often navigate by pulling up a list of all links. A link with no name is announced as just 'link', which is unusable.
commonCauses: Links wrapping images with no alt text
link-name.recommendedFix: Give every link visible text, or an aria-label when the link is icon-only.
link-name.developerGuidance: For icon links, add aria-label to the anchor and aria-hidden to the icon. For image links, ensure the image has meaningful alt text.

button-name.name: Buttons must have discernible text
button-name.description: Buttons have no accessible name, so assistive technology users cannot tell what the button does.
button-name.whyItMatters: A button announced only as 'button' forces screen reader users to guess or skip functionality entirely.
button-name.recommendedFix: Add visible text or an aria-label to every button.
button-name.developerGuidance: Every interactive control needs an accessible name. Prefer visible text; fall back to aria-label for icon-only controls.

html-has-lang.name: The <html> element must have a lang attribute
html-has-lang.description: The page does not declare its language, so screen readers may read content with the wrong pronunciation rules.
html-has-lang.whyItMatters: Screen readers use the lang attribute to choose the correct speech synthesizer voice and pronunciation. The wrong language makes content unintelligible.
commonCauses: Server-rendered pages built without the attribute
html-has-lang.recommendedFix: Add lang to the root html element matching the page's primary language.
html-has-lang.developerGuidance: Set lang once in your root layout or document template. Use regional subtags (en-GB, pt-BR) when pronunciation differs.

document-title.name: Documents must have a title element
document-title.description: The page has no <title>, so users cannot identify it in tabs, bookmarks, or screen reader announcements.
document-title.whyItMatters: The title is the first thing announced when a page loads with a screen reader, and it identifies pages in browser tabs and history.
commonCauses: Single-page apps that never set document.title
document-title.recommendedFix: Add a descriptive, unique <title> to every page.
document-title.developerGuidance: In Next.js, export metadata with a title per route. Make titles unique and front-load the page-specific part.

label.name: Form elements must have labels
label.description: Form inputs have no associated label, so assistive technology users cannot tell what information to enter.
label.whyItMatters: Without labels, screen readers announce inputs as just 'edit text', and voice-control users cannot target fields by name.
commonCauses: Placeholder text used instead of labels
Custom form components missing name wiring
label.recommendedFix: Associate a visible <label> with every input using for/id, or wrap the input in the label.
label.developerGuidance: Placeholders disappear on input and are not a substitute for labels. Always render a programmatically-associated visible label.

heading-order.name: Heading levels should only increase by one
heading-order.description: Headings skip levels (e.g. h1 to h4), breaking the document outline that screen reader users navigate by.
heading-order.whyItMatters: Screen reader users jump between headings to skim pages. Skipped levels make the structure confusing and content easy to miss.
commonCauses: Choosing heading tags for their size rather than meaning
heading-order.recommendedFix: Structure headings hierarchically (h1 → h2 → h3) and style them with CSS instead of picking tags by size.
heading-order.developerGuidance: Decouple heading semantics from visual size. If a component needs a smaller look, keep the correct tag and restyle it.

region.name: All page content should be contained by landmarks
region.description: Content exists outside landmark regions (main, nav, header, footer), making it hard to navigate with assistive technology.
region.whyItMatters: Landmarks let screen reader users jump directly to the main content or navigation instead of reading the page top to bottom.
commonCauses: Content placed directly in body outside semantic containers
region.recommendedFix: Wrap page content in semantic landmark elements: header, nav, main, aside, footer.
region.developerGuidance: Every page should have exactly one main. Replace wrapper divs with semantic elements — same styling hooks, better structure.

duplicate-id-aria.name: IDs used in ARIA must be unique
duplicate-id-aria.description: Duplicate id values are referenced by ARIA attributes, so assistive technology may associate the wrong element.
duplicate-id-aria.whyItMatters: aria-labelledby and aria-describedby resolve to the first matching id. Duplicates cause wrong or missing announcements.
duplicate-id-aria.recommendedFix: Ensure every id referenced by ARIA attributes is unique in the document.
duplicate-id-aria.developerGuidance: In React, generate ids with useId instead of hardcoding them inside reusable components.

meta-viewport.name: Zooming and scaling must not be disabled
meta-viewport.description: The viewport meta tag disables pinch-to-zoom, preventing low-vision users from magnifying content.
meta-viewport.whyItMatters: Many users rely on zoom to read text. Disabling it makes content inaccessible on mobile devices.
commonCauses: user-scalable=no added to prevent layout shifts
meta-viewport.recommendedFix: Remove user-scalable=no and maximum-scale restrictions from the viewport meta tag.
meta-viewport.developerGuidance: Fix layout issues with CSS rather than locking zoom. Users must always be able to scale to at least 200%.

frame-title.name: Frames must have an accessible name
frame-title.description: iframe elements have no title, so screen reader users cannot tell what embedded content contains.
frame-title.whyItMatters: Screen readers announce iframes by their title. Without one, users hear only 'frame' and must enter it blindly to find out what it is.
commonCauses: Embedded videos and maps without titles
frame-title.recommendedFix: Add a descriptive title attribute to every iframe.
frame-title.codeExample: <iframe src="https://maps.example.com/…" title="Map showing our office location" />
frame-title.developerGuidance: Give every user-facing iframe a title describing its content. Hide purely technical iframes with aria-hidden and tabindex=-1.

list.name: Lists must be structured correctly
list.description: ul/ol elements contain children other than li, breaking list semantics for assistive technology.
list.whyItMatters: Screen readers announce list length and position ('list, 5 items'). Invalid structure breaks these announcements.
commonCauses: Wrapper divs placed directly inside ul
Custom list components emitting invalid markup
list.recommendedFix: Only li (and script/template) elements may be direct children of ul/ol.
list.developerGuidance: Move wrapper elements inside the li rather than between the ul and li.

aria-required-attr.name: Required ARIA attributes must be provided
aria-required-attr.description: Elements with ARIA roles are missing attributes those roles require, producing broken semantics.
aria-required-attr.whyItMatters: A role="checkbox" without aria-checked tells a screen reader user there is a checkbox but never reveals its state.
commonCauses: Custom widgets built with divs and roles but missing state attributes
aria-required-attr.recommendedFix: Provide every attribute the role requires, or use the native HTML element that gets it for free.
aria-required-attr.developerGuidance: Prefer native elements over ARIA recreations. If you must use roles, consult the ARIA spec for each role's required states.

nested-interactive.name: Interactive controls must not be nested
nested-interactive.description: Focusable elements are nested inside other interactive controls, producing unpredictable keyboard and screen reader behavior.
nested-interactive.whyItMatters: A button inside a link confuses both keyboard navigation order and what action actually fires, and some screen readers only expose the outer control.
commonCauses: Clickable cards wrapping buttons in anchors
nested-interactive.recommendedFix: Restructure so interactive elements are siblings, not ancestors of one another.
nested-interactive.developerGuidance: For clickable cards, use a single primary link and absolutely position it, keeping secondary actions as sibling elements.

ml-low-quality-alt-text.name: Alt text present but low quality (ML-classified)
ml-low-quality-alt-text.description: Images have alt attributes, so deterministic checkers pass them — but a text-quality classifier judged the alt text generic, redundant, or uninformative.
ml-low-quality-alt-text.whyItMatters: alt="image" or alt="photo.jpg" technically satisfies checkers while giving screen reader users no real information. Quality matters as much as presence.
ml-low-quality-alt-text.recommendedFix: Rewrite alt text to describe the image's information or function in context, in one concise sentence.
ml-low-quality-alt-text.developerGuidance: Ask: what would I say aloud to describe this image to someone on the phone? That sentence is your alt text.

ml-generic-link-text.name: Generic link text (ML-classified)
ml-generic-link-text.description: Links have text, so deterministic checkers pass them — but a classifier judged the text generic ('click here', 'read more'), which is meaningless out of context.
ml-generic-link-text.whyItMatters: Screen reader users navigate by listing all links. Ten links that all say 'read more' are indistinguishable.
commonCauses: Card patterns with uniform 'Learn more' links
ml-generic-link-text.recommendedFix: Make link text describe the destination: 'Read the Q3 report' instead of 'Read more'.
ml-generic-link-text.codeExample: See pricing plans Read more about the Q3 accessibility report
ml-generic-link-text.developerGuidance: If the visual design demands short link text, append screen-reader-only context with a visually hidden span.

ml-generic-button-label.name: Vague button label (ML-classified)
ml-generic-button-label.description: Buttons have labels, so deterministic checkers pass them — but a classifier judged the label too vague ('go', 'submit', 'ok') to convey the action.
ml-generic-button-label.whyItMatters: Voice-control users say button names to activate them, and screen reader users rely on labels to predict what will happen. Vague labels cause mistakes.
ml-generic-button-label.recommendedFix: Label buttons with the specific action: 'Save changes', 'Delete account', 'Send message'.
ml-generic-button-label.developerGuidance: A good label answers 'what happens when I press this?' without needing surrounding context.
